study_identification_part.si4_title: Age-Associated Deviations of Amygdala Functional Connectivity in Youths With Psychosis Spectrum Disorders: Relevance to Psychotic Symptoms

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To create normative growth charts of amygdala functional connectivity in typically developing youths, assess age-associated deviations of these trajectories in youths with psychosis spectrum disorders, and explore how these disruptions are related to clinical symptomatology.
study_characteristics_part.sc3_study_design_other: Mixed: primarily cross-sectional (3 samples) with one longitudinal sample (Luna 1 with 1-3 visits per participant)

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Brain maturation deviation score: absolute value of the difference between individual's observed connectivity and predicted 'normative' connectivity based on the best-fit developmental model for controls
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The study used a brain maturation deviation score approach. For each individual in the psychosis spectrum group, they predicted what the expected 'normative' connectivity value would be based on the model fitted to typically developing controls, then subtracted this predicted value from the actual observed value and took the absolute value. This created an age-independent deviation metric that quantifies how far each individual deviates from the normative trajectory regardless of direction.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: Using the model of best fit for developmental changes observed for amygdala connectivity in the typically developing control group, we predicted what the expected 'normative' amygdala connectivity value would be for the psychosis spectrum group. We then subtracted the predicted value from the actual amygdala connectivity value for each individual and took the absolute value of this score. This created an amygdala connectivity maturation deviation score, a method that has been used previously to identify deviations from normative growth in brain connectivity metrics.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear mixed-effects models with inverse age-by-group interaction terms were used to test age-associated deviations in psychosis spectrum and other psychopathology groups compared to controls. Fixed effects included: inverse age, group, inverse age × group interaction, site, sex, and framewise displacement. Subject was included as random effect. Multiple comparison correction used false discovery rate (FDR) method (q<0.1 for significant clusters). Simple slopes analyses conducted using least-squares means (lsmeans package) to examine group differences at specific ages. Voxelwise exploratory analyses used 3dLME with age-by-group interaction (p<0.001, cluster-wise p=0.05, 30 continuous voxels minimum). For symptom associations: Pearson correlations between brain maturation deviation scores and positive symptoms in psychosis spectrum group (FDR correction, q<0.1). Post hoc directional analyses: after regressing out age, sex, and motion covariates, Pearson correlations computed between connectivity values and positive symptoms during specific developmental periods where groups significantly differed.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Youths with psychosis spectrum disorders exhibited failed normative age-related decreases in centromedial amygdala connectivity with prefrontal cortices, striatum, thalamus, and occipital cortex; age-related deviations in centromedial amygdala-striatum and centromedial amygdala-occipital connectivity were unique to psychosis spectrum group; greater age-related deviation in centromedial amygdala-thalamus connectivity was associated with increased positive symptom severity.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study established normative developmental trajectories showing significant age-related decreases in centromedial amygdala connectivity with 19 brain clusters in typically developing youths (N=622, ages 10-25). The inverse form of age provided the best model fit for all significant clusters. Youths with psychosis spectrum disorders (N=194) failed to show typical age-associated decreases in six key regions: left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (cluster 11, χ²=7.5, p=0.006, q=0.04), left putamen (cluster 12, χ²=8.2, p=0.004, q=0.04), left caudate (cluster 16, χ²=8.5, p=0.004, q=0.04), right thalamus (cluster 14, χ²=6.7, p=0.009, q=0.05), left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (cluster 17, χ²=4.1, p=0.04, q=0.09), and right middle occipital cortex (cluster 19, χ²=5.4, p=0.02, q=0.05). During late childhood/early adolescence, the psychosis spectrum group exhibited significantly lower connectivity compared to controls in five of these regions, while in adulthood they showed higher connectivity (reflecting lack of developmental decreases). Two connectivity alterations were specific to psychosis spectrum disorders compared to both controls and other psychopathology (N=246): centromedial amygdala-putamen and centromedial amygdala-occipital cortex connectivity. Greater deviation from normative centromedial amygdala-thalamus connectivity was associated with increased positive symptom severity (r=0.19, p=0.01, q=0.05), particularly with grandiose ideas (r=0.31, p<0.001) and hallucinations (r=0.23, p=0.003). During late childhood/early adolescence (ages 10-15), lower amygdala-thalamus connectivity correlated with greater positive symptoms (r=-0.27, p=0.01, q=0.05). All significant age-by-group interactions remained when psychiatric medication status was included as covariate and when the other psychopathology group was added to models.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional data for clinical groups (cannot definitively show altered development vs abnormalities due to psychosis onset); lack of longitudinal data for psychosis spectrum group prevents assessment of within-person change; nonlinear developmental patterns most accurately captured with longitudinal analyses; dynamic changes in psychotic symptoms over time not accounted for; site effects present despite statistical control (may have obscured smaller developmental changes or subtle group differences); differences in task instructions, MRI resolution, and scan duration across sites; cross-sectional design cannot distinguish between accelerated developmental decrease vs deterioration of circuitry
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Our study was limited by the fact that cross-sectional data were available only for the psychosis spectrum group. Thus, the neurodevelopmental trajectories in psychosis spectrum disorders do not reflect within-person change. Our cross-sectional sample cannot definitively show whether our results are due to altered development or abnormalities due to time of onset of psychosis... many developmental changes that occur during adolescence are nonlinear, and these patterns are most accurately captured with longitudinal analyses. Additionally, psychotic symptoms are dynamic and change over time, and these changes need to be taken into account when characterizing neurodevelopmental change... while we are fairly confident that we were able to appropriately account for site in our analyses (see Figure S4), we observed a statistically significant effect of site in many of the regions of interest (see Table S4). Despite all scans being performed on the same scanner model, there were still differences in task instructions, MRI resolution, and duration of scan. Site effects may have obscured our ability to identify smaller developmental changes in normative amygdala connectivity developmental trajectories. It is also possible that we failed to identify more subtle age-related deviations in amygdala connectivity between the psychosis spectrum and typically developing groups because of site effects.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study demonstrates proof-of-principle for merging multiple resting-state fMRI datasets to create normative developmental trajectories. Age-associated changes were remarkably consistent across different control samples despite multiple sites, protocols, and recruitment methods (Figure S3). Growth charting methodology extended from physical metrics (weight, head circumference) to brain connectivity metrics. Developmental specificity examined by comparing psychosis spectrum to other psychopathology group, revealing two connectivity patterns unique to psychosis (amygdala-putamen, amygdala-occipital). Time-varying developmental effects: group differences emerged during specific developmental windows (late childhood/early adolescence for underconnectivity; adulthood for lack of normative decreases). Post hoc symptom analyses stratified by developmental period to identify when connectivity-symptom relationships were strongest. All analyses controlled for psychiatric medication status.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is one of the earlier applications of normative modeling growth chart methodology to resting-state fMRI connectivity data in psychiatry (2019). The study used a 'big data' approach by aggregating four samples to achieve N=622 controls, which was relatively large for that time period. The inverse age transformation (rather than linear or quadratic) provided best model fit across all 19 significant centromedial amygdala connectivity clusters and the 1 basolateral amygdala cluster, suggesting non-linear developmental trajectories that are steeper in childhood and plateau in adulthood. The study focused specifically on amygdala subregions (centromedial vs basolateral) based on previous work by the authors showing differential developmental trajectories. Psychiatric diagnoses for Pitt cohort determined via SCID; for Philadelphia cohort via computerized GOASSESS based on KSADS-PL, with psychosis spectrum defined via SIPS/PS-R criteria. Other psychopathology group defined as meeting DSM-IV criteria for non-psychotic disorder with significant distress/impairment (rating >5 on 0-10 scale). One longitudinal cohort (Luna 1) with 1-3 visits per participant; remaining three cohorts were cross-sectional. All scans acquired on Siemens 3T Tim Trio scanners but with protocol differences across sites (see Table S2). Sensitivity analyses confirmed that all significant developmental effects remained when motion covariates included and when high-motion subjects excluded, and when MRI software version was included in model.
